lessons.title: Scalars and Vectors
lessons.content:
In physics, we categorise quantities into two types: scalars and vectors. A scalar quantity has magnitude (size) only. Examples include mass, time, temperature, and speed. A vector quantity, however, has both magnitude AND direction. Examples include force, displacement, velocity, and acceleration. This distinction is crucial because vectors must be combined differently than simple numbers.

When adding vectors, you cannot simply add their magnitudes unless they are in the same direction. Instead, we use methods like the 'head-to-tail' rule or the 'parallelogram law' to find the resultant vector. For example, if you walk 3 metres east and then 4 metres north, your total distance is 7 metres (scalar), but your displacement is 5 metres at a specific angle (vector), calculated using Pythagoras' theorem.

Mastering vectors is the first step in understanding mechanics. In the CSEC exam, you will often be asked to represent vectors as arrows, resolve them into horizontal and vertical components, and calculate the resultant force or velocity in various scenarios.

Add vectors graphically and algebraically

Vectors have magnitude and direction (e.g., force, velocity).

lessons.title: Distance-Time and Velocity-Time Graphs
lessons.content:
Graphs are powerful tools for visualising and analysing motion. A distance-time graph plots distance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. The gradient (slope) of the line at any point represents the speed of the object. A straight line indicates constant speed, while a curved line indicates changing speed (acceleration). A horizontal line means the object is stationary.

A velocity-time graph provides even more information. The gradient of the line represents the acceleration of the object. Like distance-time graphs, a straight line indicates constant acceleration, and a horizontal line indicates constant velocity. Most importantly, the area under the velocity-time graph represents the total displacement (distance moved in a specific direction) of the object.

To excel in CSEC Physics, you must be comfortable calculating gradients and areas for different graph shapes. For a constant acceleration (a straight line), the area is usually a triangle or a trapezium. Remember: always check the units on the axes before starting your calculations!

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
lessons.content:
A force is a push or a pull measured in newtons (N). Forces can change an object's speed, direction or shape, and the overall force on an object is the resultant force: forces acting in the same direction add, forces acting in opposite directions subtract. Balanced (zero resultant) forces mean no change in motion; unbalanced forces mean acceleration.

Newton's three laws explain this. First law: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless an unbalanced force acts on it (often called the law of inertia). Second law: the resultant force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma. Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, acting on a different object.

Momentum is mass times velocity (p = mv) and is a vector. In a collision or explosion the total momentum before equals the total momentum after (conservation of momentum), provided no external resultant force acts. Friction is the force that opposes motion between surfaces, and it transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy.

Calculate resultant force and use F = ma

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Power
lessons.content:
Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force: work done = force x distance moved (in the direction of the force), measured in joules (J). One joule is one newton-metre.

Energy is the ability to do work, measured in joules, and it is conserved: energy is transferred from one store to another but never created or destroyed. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, KE = 1/2 mv squared. Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored by height, GPE = mgh. Falling objects transfer GPE to KE, and in a closed system the totals match.

Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = work done / time taken, measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. Efficiency compares useful output with total input: efficiency = useful energy or power output / total input x 100 per cent. Wasted energy is usually transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy. Simple machines such as levers and pulleys do not reduce the work needed; they reduce the force needed by increasing the distance over which it acts.

Energy sources: renewable and non-renewable. A renewable energy source is one that is replaced naturally, so it will not be used up as long as the Sun keeps shining: solar, wind, hydroelectric, wave and tidal, geothermal and biomass. A non-renewable energy source is one that is used up much faster than it can be replaced: coal, crude oil and natural gas (the fossil fuels), and nuclear fuels such as uranium. The fossil fuels were formed from the remains of living things over millions of years, and burning them releases carbon dioxide, so they are also described as polluting.

The sources are used in different ways: a solar panel transfers light energy into electrical energy, a wind turbine or a hydroelectric station transfers the kinetic energy of moving air or water into electrical energy, and geothermal energy uses thermal energy from deep inside the Earth. Hydroelectric and wind power depend on rainfall or on the weather, and a large scheme can flood land or change the course of a river; a fuel such as coal, oil or gas can be stored and burned whenever energy is needed. In a question on energy sources, read carefully which source is being asked about: the sources that are not renewable are coal, oil, natural gas and nuclear fuel, while solar, wind, hydroelectric, wave, tidal, geothermal and biomass are renewable.

lessons.title: Pressure in Fluids and Upthrust
lessons.content:
Pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A, measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m squared. A force spread over a larger area gives a smaller pressure, which is why wide tyres and foundations spread weight, while sharp edges concentrate force.

Pressure in a fluid increases with depth and with the density of the fluid: pressure = density x gravitational field strength x depth. This is why a dam wall is thicker at the bottom and why the pressure on a diver's ears increases as they descend. Atmospheric pressure decreases with height above sea level.

A body in a fluid experiences upthrust, an upward force caused by the pressure difference between the fluid pushing harder on the deeper bottom surface than on the top. Upthrust is equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle). An object floats when its weight equals the upthrust on it, and sinks when its weight is greater. A hydraulic press uses pressure transmitted through a liquid so that a small force on a small piston produces a large force on a larger piston, since the pressure is the same throughout.

Explain how pressure in a fluid varies with depth and density
State Archimedes' principle and explain floating and sinking
concepts: Pressure: force per unit area, P = F/A, measured in pascals.
Upthrust: the upward force a fluid exerts on a body in it, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.

lessons.title: Temperature and Heat Transfer
lessons.content:
Temperature and heat are related but distinct concepts. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance — it tells us how hot or cold something is. Heat is the total thermal energy that transfers from a hotter object to a colder one. This transfer continues until both objects reach the same temperature, a state known as thermal equilibrium.

There are three main mechanisms of heat transfer: conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction is the transfer of energy through direct contact between particles, mainly in solids (especially metals). Convection is the transfer of energy through the movement of fluids (liquids and gases) as warmer, less dense areas rise and cooler, denser areas sink. Radiation is the transfer of energy via electromagnetic waves, which can travel through a vacuum (like heat from the sun reaching Earth).

In the CSEC syllabus, you will study how different materials act as conductors or insulators and how these principles are applied in everyday life, from cooking utensils to home insulation. You will also learn about the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales and how to convert between them.

The idea of heat has a history worth knowing, because it shows how a physical theory is replaced by a better one. Until the late eighteenth century most scientists explained heating with a caloric theory: heat was thought to be a weightless fluid, called caloric, that flowed out of a hot body into a cold one. On that view a hot cup of tea held more caloric than a cold one, and rubbing two surfaces together squeezed caloric out of them. The theory explained a good deal, and it is the reason we still say that energy is transferred from hot to cold.

Count Rumford's boring of cannon barrels in the 1790s weakened it: the drilling went on producing heat for as long as the work continued, and no fluid could be supplied for ever. Later measurements of the mechanical equivalent of heat showed that work and heat are both energy, and that led to the kinetic theory: heat is the energy of the random motion of the particles of a substance, and temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of those particles. The caloric theory is the historical heat theory that the kinetic theory replaced, and the two are contrasted whenever a question asks what heat actually is.
objectives: Define temperature and heat
Describe conduction, convection, and radiation

Conduction occurs in solids; Convection in fluids; Radiation in vacuum.
The caloric theory treated heat as a weightless fluid, caloric, that flowed from a hot body into a cold one.
The kinetic theory replaced the caloric theory: heat is the energy of the random motion of the particles, and temperature measures their average kinetic energy.
Count Rumford's cannon boring produced heat without limit for as long as the work went on, which a fluid could not explain.

lessons.title: The Gas Laws
lessons.content:
The behaviour of gases can be described by three fundamental laws that relate pressure (P), volume (V), and temperature (T). Boyle's Law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂). This means if you decrease the volume of a container by half, the pressure of the gas inside will double.

Charles' Law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂). The Pressure Law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂). Note that for these laws, temperature MUST be measured in Kelvin (K = °C + 273).

These laws are combined into the General Gas Law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. On the CSEC exam, you will use these formulas to predict how a gas will react to changes in its environment. Understanding the kinetic theory of gases — that gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of their container — will help you visualise why these relationships exist.

The Kelvin temperature scale is the absolute scale, and it is the scale the gas laws are written in. Its zero is absolute zero, written 0 K and equal to -273 degrees Celsius, the temperature at which a gas would have no thermal energy left to give and its pressure would fall to zero. One kelvin is exactly the same size as one degree Celsius, so a change of temperature is the same number in both scales; only the zero point differs. Converting is a single step: K = degrees Celsius + 273, and degrees Celsius = K - 273. A room at 27 degrees Celsius is 300 K, and water boiling at 100 degrees Celsius is 373 K.

The gas laws must use the Kelvin scale, because each law says that pressure, or volume, is directly proportional to temperature, and a direct proportion only holds when the scale starts at zero. Doubling 27 degrees Celsius to 54 degrees Celsius does not double the pressure of a fixed mass of gas, but doubling 300 K to 600 K does. Substituting a negative Celsius temperature would give a negative pressure, which is nonsense - another sign that the Celsius zero is arbitrary, fixed at the ice point, while the Kelvin zero is the lowest temperature that can exist.

Kinetic theory explains all three gas laws with one picture: a gas is a very large number of particles in rapid random motion, the pressure on the walls of the container is the total force of the particles colliding with those walls, and the temperature is the average kinetic energy of the particles.

Boyle's Law follows because squeezing a fixed mass of gas into half its volume leaves the particles twice as crowded, so they strike the walls twice as often and the pressure doubles at constant temperature. Charles' Law follows because heating the gas raises the average kinetic energy of the particles, so each one hits the walls harder and more often, and the gas expands at constant pressure until the pressure has fallen back to what it was. The Pressure Law follows for a fixed volume held in a rigid container: heating raises the average kinetic energy, the collisions become more forceful and more frequent, and the pressure rises.

Absolute zero fits the same picture, because at 0 K the particles would have no kinetic energy left and the pressure would be zero. Real gases turn into liquids before that point is reached, which is why the gas laws are called ideal gas laws and are most accurate for a gas well above its boiling point and not compressed near to liquefying.

The gas laws need the Kelvin scale because a direct proportion between pressure or volume and temperature is only true when the scale starts at zero.
Gas pressure is the force of the gas particles colliding with the walls of their container.
Heating a gas raises the average kinetic energy of its particles, so the collisions with the walls become more frequent and more forceful.
Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and the Pressure Law are all explained by the motion of the particles of the gas.

lessons.title: Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
lessons.content:
Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius, measured in J/kg degrees Celsius. Water has a high value (about 4200), which is why it heats and cools slowly and is used in car cooling systems. The energy transferred in heating is E = mc delta theta, where c is the specific heat capacity and delta theta is the temperature rise.

When a substance changes state, its temperature stays constant while energy is being supplied: the energy is used to break the forces between particles rather than to increase their average kinetic energy. The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy to melt 1 kg of a solid at its melting point; the specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy to boil 1 kg of a liquid at its boiling point. The energy transferred is E = mL, where L is the specific latent heat.

Condensation is the reverse of vaporisation: when a gas or a vapour cools, its particles lose energy and the forces between them pull them back together into the liquid state, and the latent heat that was absorbed at boiling is released. Steam at 100 degrees Celsius condenses to water at 100 degrees Celsius, giving out a large amount of energy as it changes, which is why a steam burn is so severe. Condensation explains the water that forms on the outside of a cold glass, the dew on grass in the early morning, and the liquid collected in the condenser of a refrigerator or a distillation apparatus.

Thermal expansion: nearly all solids, liquids and gases expand when heated and contract when cooled, because the particles vibrate more and move further apart. This is why railway lines and bridges have expansion gaps and why a bimetallic strip of two metals with different expansion rates bends when heated — a property used in thermostats and fire alarms.

The effects of thermal expansion are met in engineering and in the home. A solid expands in every direction, so a long metal rail laid without a gap buckles on a hot day, which is why railway lines have expansion gaps, and why bridge decks and concrete roads have expansion joints. A liquid expands more than its container does, and a liquid-in-glass thermometer is built on exactly that effect, because the liquid is forced up a narrow bore as it warms. A gas expands most of all, which is why a sealed tin must never be heated and why a balloon left in the sun stretches.

Expansion is also used deliberately. A bimetallic strip of two metals with different expansion rates bends when it is heated, and the bending closes an electrical contact: that is the working part of a thermostat, of a fire alarm and of the older type of electric iron. Shrink-fitting uses the effect the other way round - a metal tyre or a rivet is made slightly too small, warmed so that it expands, slipped over the wheel or through the plate, and left to cool, when it grips tightly. A tight metal lid is loosened by warming it, because the metal expands more than the glass it is screwed onto.

Expansion causes trouble as well. A thick glass tumbler can crack when boiling water is poured into it, because the inside surface expands before the heat has reached the outside, and thin glass - or a metal spoon left in the glass to take some of the heat - avoids the crack. How much a solid expands depends on the material it is made of, on its original length and on the size of the temperature rise, so a long steel pipe carrying steam and the skin of an aircraft are both designed around expansion rather than against it.

Define specific latent heat and use E = mL
Explain thermal expansion and the bimetallic strip

Specific latent heat: the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature.
Condensation: the change of state from a gas to a liquid, in which the latent heat absorbed at boiling is released.
Thermal expansion: the increase in size of a substance when its temperature rises.

Effects of thermal expansion include railway lines buckling without expansion gaps, bridge expansion joints, a thick glass tumbler cracking in boiling water, and a bimetallic strip bending when heated.

lessons.title: Physical Properties and Thermometers
lessons.content:
An instrument measures temperature by using a physical property that changes in a regular way when the object is heated or cooled. Any such property is called a thermometric property, and a thermometer is built around one chosen thermometric property. A property is only useful if it changes steadily with temperature, so that equal steps on the scale mean equal changes of temperature, and if it changes by an amount large enough to be read accurately.

Several thermometric properties are in use. The volume of a liquid is the property used by a liquid-in-glass thermometer, in which the liquid expands up a fine capillary bore as it is warmed. The electrical resistance of a metal rises with temperature, and it is the property used by a platinum resistance thermometer. The electrical resistance of a semiconductor falls as it gets hotter, and it is the property used by a thermistor. The pressure of a gas at constant volume is the property used by a constant-volume gas thermometer, the most accurate type and the one used to check the others. The e.m.f. of a thermocouple is the property used by a thermocouple thermometer, and the expansion of a bimetallic strip is the property used by a bimetallic thermometer in a thermostat.

A liquid-in-glass thermometer is filled with mercury or with alcohol dyed red. Mercury is opaque and does not stick to the glass, so its thread moves cleanly and is easy to read, and it is used from about -39 degrees Celsius to about 357 degrees Celsius. Alcohol boils at about 78 degrees Celsius, so it cannot be used above that temperature, but it works far below the freezing point of mercury and it is dyed red so that it can be seen.

A clinical thermometer is a liquid-in-glass thermometer with a very short range, from about 35 degrees Celsius to about 42 degrees Celsius, because body temperature never moves far outside that range. Its scale is divided into steps of 0.1 degree Celsius so that a small change can be read, and a constriction in the bore above the bulb keeps the thread at the highest reading until the thermometer is shaken down.

A thermometer is calibrated by marking two fixed points on its scale and dividing the distance between them into equal degrees. A good thermometer must also respond quickly, be sensitive enough to show a small change of temperature, and be small enough that it does not change the temperature of what it is measuring. A resistance thermometer or a thermistor has the advantage that its sensor is small and its reading is an electrical resistance, so it can be read at a distance or recorded automatically.

Describe the physical properties used by liquid-in-glass, resistance, thermistor, gas and thermocouple thermometers

lessons.title: Celsius Scale Fixed Points
lessons.content:
A temperature scale needs two fixed points, whose temperatures do not change, so that an instrument can be marked at them and the distance between them divided up. On the Celsius scale the lower fixed point, called the ice point, is the temperature of pure melting ice at normal atmospheric pressure, and it is given the value 0 degrees Celsius. The upper fixed point, called the steam point, is the temperature of the steam above pure water boiling at normal atmospheric pressure, and it is given the value 100 degrees Celsius.

The distance between the two fixed points is divided into 100 equal parts, so one degree Celsius is one hundredth of the interval between the ice point and the steam point. To calibrate a thermometer it is placed in a funnel of crushed melting ice, the ice is stirred, and the level of the thread is marked 0; the bulb is then held in the steam above boiling water and the level is marked 100; the interval between the two marks is then divided into 100 equal degrees. A check at an intermediate temperature, against a standard thermometer, shows whether the bore is uniform along its length.

Two precautions matter. The bulb must be in the steam and not in the boiling water, because the water is slightly hotter than the steam when the thermometer itself cools the water; and the pressure must be stated, because the boiling point of water falls as the pressure falls. Water boils below 100 degrees Celsius high on a mountain and above 100 degrees Celsius in a pressure cooker, so a steam point marked at normal atmospheric pressure is only correct at that pressure.

The Celsius scale is also called the centigrade scale, from the 100 divisions between its fixed points. The Fahrenheit scale uses different fixed points: the ice point is 32 degrees Fahrenheit and the steam point is 212 degrees Fahrenheit, with 180 divisions between them, but the CSEC syllabus uses the Celsius scale. Because the Celsius zero is simply the ice point and not the lowest temperature that can exist, Celsius readings may be negative, and values below 0 degrees Celsius are common in colder countries.

lessons.title: States of Matter
lessons.content:
Matter exists in three states - solid, liquid and gas - and the difference between them lies in how the particles are arranged and how they move. In a solid the particles are packed closely in a regular pattern and held by strong forces, so its particles can only vibrate about a fixed position. In a liquid the particles are still close together but the forces between them are weaker, so the particles can slide past one another and the liquid can flow. In a gas the particles are far apart and the forces between them are negligible, so they move rapidly and randomly in all directions.

These arrangements explain the properties of the three states. A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, and it cannot be compressed except by a very large force. A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape, because it takes the shape of the container it is poured into, and it is very difficult to compress. A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume, because it fills its container completely, and it is easily compressed because of the large empty space between its particles.

Density follows the same picture. A solid is usually the densest state of a substance, a gas is the least dense state of a substance by a wide margin, and a liquid lies between them, because the particles of a gas are spread through a much larger volume. Diffusion, the spreading of one substance through another, is fastest in gases. Diffusion is slower in liquids and very slow in solids, because the particles of a gas move fastest and have the most space to move through.

Water is the important exception to the density rule: ice is less dense than water and so ice floats, because water expands as it freezes. Heating moves a substance from one state to a less orderly one. Melting, boiling and evaporation all take in energy that is used to break the forces holding the particles together rather than to raise the temperature, so the temperature stays constant while the change of state is going on. Sublimation takes a solid straight to a gas, as dry ice does. The random jiggling of smoke or pollen grains seen under a microscope, called Brownian motion, is evidence that the particles of a fluid are in constant random motion.

Explain the shape, volume and compressibility of each state in terms of its particles

In a liquid the particles can slide past one another and the liquid can flow, and in a gas the particles are far apart and move rapidly and randomly.
A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, a liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape, and a gas fills its container completely.
Diffusion is fastest in gases because their particles move fastest and have the most space to move through.
Brownian motion is evidence that the particles of a fluid are in constant random motion.

lessons.title: Determination of Specific Heat Capacity
lessons.content:
The specific heat capacity of a metal can be measured with an electrical heater. A block of the metal has two holes, one for the heater and one for the thermometer, and the mass of the block is found on a balance. The heater is connected to a voltmeter and an ammeter and switched on, and the voltmeter reading, the ammeter reading and the time for which the heater is switched on are all recorded. The energy supplied by the heater is the electrical energy E = VIt, where V is the potential difference in volts, I is the current in amperes and t is the time in seconds.

The temperature is read before the heater is switched on and again after it has risen by about ten degrees, so the temperature rise is the difference between the two readings. Rearranging E = mc delta theta gives the specific heat capacity as the energy supplied divided by the mass of the block and the temperature rise, that is c = VIt divided by m delta theta. A check against the accepted value shows how good the experiment was: aluminium comes out near 900 joules per kilogram degree Celsius and copper near 390.

Heat loss to the surroundings is the main source of error, and the experiment reduces it in three ways. The block is lagged with insulating material, so that little energy escapes to the air. The block starts a few degrees below room temperature and ends a few degrees above it, so the energy gained from the room at the start roughly cancels the energy lost to the room at the end. The heater is switched off just before the final reading and the highest temperature reached is taken, because the block goes on warming for a moment as the heat spreads through it.

A second method, the method of mixtures, measures the specific heat capacity of a solid that cannot easily be drilled. The solid is heated in boiling water to a known temperature and then transferred quickly into a known mass of cold water in a copper calorimeter, and the highest temperature the mixture reaches is noted. The heat lost by the hot solid equals the heat gained by the water and the calorimeter, so the specific heat capacity of the solid is found by equating the two amounts of energy. The solid must be transferred quickly, the calorimeter must be insulated, and the water must be stirred, because heat lost on the way and an uneven temperature both make the answer too low.

lessons.title: Determination of Specific Latent Heat
lessons.content:
The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is measured by melting ice with an electrical heater and weighing the water that is produced. The gauze and funnel hold the ice so that the melted water can be collected in a beaker below. An electrical heater supplies the energy E = VIt that melts the ice, and the ice is only ever at 0 degrees Celsius, so every joule supplied goes into melting ice rather than into warming it.

The steps are simple to write down. Dried crushed ice is used so that surface water is not weighed as if it had been melted by the heater. The heater is switched on and a stopwatch started, and the voltmeter reading, the ammeter reading and the time are recorded. The mass of ice melted is found by weighing the water collected while the heater is running, so that ice melted by the warmth of the room is not counted. When enough water has been collected the supply is switched off, the water is weighed, and the specific latent heat is found from L = E divided by m, the energy supplied divided by the mass of ice melted.

The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to melt one kilogram of ice at 0 degrees Celsius, about 334 000 joules per kilogram, and the same amount of energy is given out when one kilogram of water freezes. The ice must be crushed and patted dry before it is used, because surface water would be weighed as though the heater had melted it and would make the answer too small. The funnel must not be warmed by the heater, none of the collected water may be allowed to evaporate, and a large mass of ice is used so that the percentage error in weighing is small.

The specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to boil one kilogram of water, about 2 260 000 joules per kilogram, and it is much larger than the latent heat of fusion because the particles must be completely separated rather than merely loosened from one another. It is measured by passing a known electrical energy into water that is already boiling in a flask and collecting the steam that escapes in a condenser. The experiment is harder to control, because steam escapes unseen and hot apparatus is a scalding hazard, so the mass of water lost is found by weighing the flask before and after the run, and the value found is checked against the accepted one.

lessons.title: Evaporation and Boiling
lessons.content:
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into a vapour at any temperature. It happens only at the surface of the liquid, it needs no bubbles, and it takes place in an open container at whatever temperature the liquid happens to be. Boiling is the change of a liquid into a vapour at the boiling point, and it happens throughout the liquid, because bubbles of vapour form below the surface, rise and burst as they reach it. Both are vaporisation and both take in latent heat, but the two processes differ in their temperature, in where they happen and in what the liquid does afterwards.

The liquid that is left behind is cooled, because the fastest particles escape from the surface. The particles of a liquid have a range of kinetic energies, so the particles that escape are the fastest ones, the average kinetic energy of the particles remaining falls, and the temperature of the liquid falls with it. That is why a wet hand feels cold in a breeze, why sweating cools the body, why water in a porous earthenware pot stays cooler than water in a metal can, and why a refrigerator works by evaporating a volatile refrigerant in a coil inside it.

Four factors change the rate of evaporation. A higher temperature gives more particles the energy to escape from the surface. A larger surface area lets more particles escape at once. A draught of moving air carries the escaped vapour away and keeps the space above the liquid dry. Lower humidity of the air, because dry air holds fewer vapour particles already, lets evaporation continue quickly. A volatile liquid such as petrol or ether evaporates faster than water for the same reason.

Boiling happens at a definite temperature, the boiling point. The temperature stays constant while the liquid boils, because the energy supplied is used as latent heat rather than to raise the temperature. Its temperature depends on the pressure above the liquid. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at normal atmospheric pressure, at a lower temperature high on a mountain where the pressure is less, and at a higher temperature in a pressure cooker where the pressure is greater. Evaporation, by contrast, has no fixed temperature at all, because it goes on at every temperature the liquid can exist at.

Explain cooling by evaporation in terms of the escape of the fastest particles
List the factors that change the rate of evaporation, and say how pressure changes the boiling point

Evaporation cools the liquid that is left behind, because the fastest particles escape and the average kinetic energy of the particles remaining falls.

lessons.title: Absorption and Emission of Radiation Factors
lessons.content:
Every object with a temperature above absolute zero absorbs and emits infra-red radiation, and it does both at the same time. Radiation needs no medium, so it travels through a vacuum at the speed of light, and it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted when it meets a surface. Whether a surface warms or cools depends on the balance between the two: an object hotter than its surroundings emits more than it absorbs and cools down, while an object cooler than its surroundings absorbs more than it emits and warms up. When the two rates are equal the object is in thermal equilibrium with its surroundings.

The rate at which a surface absorbs or emits radiation depends on its colour and texture. A dull black surface is the best absorber, because it reflects almost nothing, and it is also the best emitter. A shiny, silvered surface is a poor absorber, because it reflects most of the radiation that falls on it, and it is also a poor emitter. White and light surfaces reflect most of the radiation that falls on them and absorb little. A rough, matt surface has a larger real area than a smooth one, so it absorbs and emits more than a polished surface of the same size.

The temperature of the object is the second factor. The hotter an object is, the more radiation it emits each second, so a hot object loses energy faster than a warm one. The rate of emission falls as the object cools, and it becomes equal to the rate at which it absorbs when the object reaches the temperature of its surroundings, at which point it stops losing temperature by radiation.

The area of the surface is the third factor. A large surface area emits and absorbs more radiation each second than a small one at the same temperature, which is why a car radiator and the elements of a heater are built with a large area, and why a thin wire cools faster than a thick one. The factors are studied with Leslie's cube, a metal cube whose vertical faces are dull black, white and silvered, filled with hot water, with a radiation detector held near each face in turn: the face that gives the strongest reading is the dull black one, and the silvered face gives the weakest.

Describe how colour, texture, temperature and area change the rate of absorption and emission

lessons.title: Good Absorbers and Emitters
lessons.content:
A surface that absorbs radiation well also emits it well, and a surface that reflects radiation well absorbs and emits it poorly. Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of radiation. Shiny, silvered or white surfaces are poor absorbers and poor emitters, because they reflect radiation instead of taking it in. The same surface behaves the same way in both directions, so the black base of a cooking pot takes in the energy of a flame quickly, and that same black surface, when it is hot, gives out energy quickly.

This single rule explains many everyday designs. A vacuum flask, also called a Dewar flask, is silvered inside so that its walls are poor emitters and poor absorbers of radiation, and it is double-walled with the air pumped out so that there is nothing between the walls to conduct or to convect; a cork or plastic stopper closes the top, because both are poor conductors. Tea in a silvered pot stays hot for the same reason, because the shiny surface radiates very little, and the same pot keeps a cold drink cold, because a shiny surface also absorbs very little radiation from the warm room.

A solar water heater uses the opposite choice. The plate of a solar water heater is painted matt black so that it absorbs as much of the sun's radiation as possible, and it is covered by glass, which lets the short-wave radiation of the sun in and slows down the escape of the longer-wave radiation given out by the hot plate. A greenhouse and a closed car left standing in the sun are warmed by the same trap.

Other applications follow the rule. The radiator of a car and the fins of an electric heater are painted black so that they emit as strongly as possible, and a heater is placed in front of a shiny reflector so that most of its radiation is directed into the room instead of into the wall behind it. White clothes are worn in strong sunshine, because a white surface reflects the sun's radiation and absorbs little, and dark clothes feel hotter for the opposite reason. An engine, a hot pipe and a metal roof all lose energy by radiation, and giving them a shiny surface slows that loss.

lessons.title: Thermal Energy Transfer Device Design
lessons.content:
Designers reduce unwanted heat transfer by attacking each of the three mechanisms in turn: they choose a poor conductor to slow conduction, they trap air or remove it to stop convection, and they use shiny surfaces to cut down radiation. A good design usually does all three at once, and the same design that keeps a hot drink hot also keeps a cold drink cold, because it slows the transfer of energy in both directions.

The vacuum flask is the clearest example. It has a double wall of glass with the air pumped out of the space between, so there is no air to conduct or to convect across the gap, and both glass surfaces are silvered, which makes them poor emitters and poor absorbers of radiation. The bottle is held in a plastic case, and it is closed with a cork or plastic stopper, because both are poor conductors and the stopper also stops warm air leaving by convection at the top.

A solar water heater is designed to collect energy instead of keeping it out. Its plate is painted matt black so that it absorbs as much of the sun's radiation as possible, and it is covered by glass, which lets the short-wave radiation of the sun in and slows down the escape of the longer-wave radiation given out by the hot plate. The pipes of the plate are joined to a tank above them, and because warm water is less dense than cold water, convection carries the heated water up into the tank and brings cooler water down to be heated, so no pump is needed. The tank is lagged so that the collected energy is not lost again.

House insulation uses the same thinking. Loft insulation of fibreglass or rock wool traps air, and trapped air is a poor conductor, so energy from the rooms below cannot conduct through the roof. Cavity wall insulation fills the gap between the two leaves of a brick wall with foam or beads for the same reason, and stops convection in the cavity. Double glazing puts two sheets of glass with air or argon between them, which slows conduction and stops convection, and a foil behind a radiator sends radiation back into the room. Draught excluders, heavy curtains and closed doors cut down convection, because moving air carries energy away faster than any other mechanism. A cooking pan follows the same rules from the other side: a metal base conducts energy well into the food, and a wooden or plastic handle is a poor conductor, so that the pan can be lifted.

lessons.title: Properties of Waves
lessons.content:
A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Waves are classified into two main types: transverse and longitudinal. In a transverse wave (like light or water waves), the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of energy travel. In a longitudinal wave (like sound), the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy travel, creating areas of compression and rarefaction.

Key wave properties include amplitude (maximum displacement from rest), wavelength (distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs), and frequency (the number of waves passing a point per second). The relationship between these is given by the wave equation: Speed (v) = Frequency (f) × Wavelength (λ).

Waves also undergo four important behaviours: reflection (bouncing off a surface), refraction (changing direction when entering a new medium), diffraction (spreading out when passing through a gap), and interference (two waves overlapping). The CSEC exam often uses ripple tanks to demonstrate these properties and asks you to apply the wave equation to solve problems.

lessons.title: Refraction and Lenses
lessons.content:
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another of different optical density. This happens because light changes speed. When light enters a denser medium (like from air into glass), it slows down and bends toward the normal line. The degree of bending is described by Snell's Law: n = sin(i) / sin(r), where n is the refractive index of the medium.

Lenses use refraction to focus or spread light. A converging (convex) lens is thicker in the middle and bends light rays together to a focal point. It can form both real and virtual images. A diverging (concave) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads light rays apart, always forming a virtual, upright, and diminished image.

You will learn to draw ray diagrams to locate images formed by lenses and understand how they are used in devices like cameras, magnifying glasses, and the human eye. CSEC questions frequently involve calculating the refractive index or using the lens formula to find image distance and magnification.

In a ray diagram, the light travelling towards the boundary is the incident ray and the ray leaving on the other side is the refracted ray. The angle of incidence i is measured between the incident ray and the normal, and the angle of refraction r between the refracted ray and the normal: in the diagram below i = 48.6 degrees and r = 30 degrees, so n = sin 48.6 / sin 30 = 1.5.

figures.alt: A ray of light meeting an air-glass boundary at the normal, with the angle of incidence marked as 48.6 degrees in air and the angle of refraction marked as 30 degrees inside the glass, beside a converging lens bringing parallel rays to its focal point and a diverging lens spreading them apart.
figures.caption: Snell's Law in one picture: n = sin i / sin r = sin 48.6 / sin 30 = 1.5, so light entering the denser medium bends toward the normal.

lessons.title: Reflection and Total Internal Reflection
lessons.content:
When light reflects off a plane surface, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface). The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright, laterally inverted and the same size as the object, and it appears the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

Concave and convex mirrors are curved reflectors. A concave (converging) mirror brings parallel rays to a focus and can form a real image; a convex (diverging) mirror spreads rays and always forms a virtual, diminished image, which is why it gives a wide field of view in drivers' mirrors and shop security mirrors.

When light travels from a denser medium such as glass or water into a less dense medium such as air, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases there comes an angle — the critical angle — beyond which no light refracts out; it all reflects back inside the medium. This is total internal reflection, and it is used in optical fibres to carry light and signals along a curved path, and in prisms in binoculars. A prism also disperses white light into a spectrum, because each colour refracts by a different amount.

lessons.title: Sound and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.content:
Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium: it travels by compressing and rarefying the particles of a solid, liquid or gas, and cannot travel through a vacuum. In air at room temperature sound travels at about 330-340 m/s, much slower than light. Speed = distance / time, so an echo — sound reflected from a distant surface such as a cliff or the sea bed — can be used to measure distance.

The pitch of a note is set by its frequency (higher frequency, higher pitch) and the loudness by its amplitude (greater amplitude, louder sound). The human ear hears roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, and frequencies above this range are called ultrasound. Ultrasound echoes are used in medical scanning and in depth sounding.

The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves and microwaves through infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays — all transverse waves that travel through a vacuum at the speed of light (about 3 x 10 to the 8 m/s). They differ in wavelength and frequency, and the visible region is the narrow band between infrared and ultraviolet.

The electromagnetic spectrum: the family of transverse waves from radio to gamma rays that travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.

lessons.title: Current, Voltage, and Resistance
lessons.content:
Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually carried by electrons through a conductor. Current (I) is the rate of flow of charge, measured in Amperes (A). Voltage (V), or potential difference, is the energy per unit charge that 'pushes' the current through the circuit, measured in Volts (V). Resistance (R) is the opposition to the flow of current, measured in Ohms (Ω).

The relationship between these three quantities is known as Ohm's Law: V = IR. This law states that for many materials, the current is directly proportional to the voltage applied, provided the temperature remains constant. Components like resistors follow this law, while others like light bulbs change their resistance as they get hotter.

In CSEC Physics, you will build and analyse series and parallel circuits. In a series circuit, there is only one path for the current, so it remains the same everywhere. In a parallel circuit, there are multiple paths, and the total current is the sum of the currents in each branch. You will also learn to calculate total resistance for both types of arrangements and use multimeters to take measurements.

The key that comes with the diagrams names the circuit symbols used: the battery (the long plate is the positive terminal), the resistor and the bulb. In the parallel arrangement each branch is connected across the same potential difference, so the same 6 V battery drives 3 A through a 2 Ω branch and 2 A through a 3 Ω branch, a total of 5 A; in series it drives one current of 1 A through a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor, leaving 2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 4 V across the 4 Ω resistor.

lessons.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
lessons.content:
A magnet has a north and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract. Magnetic materials such as iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are attracted to a magnet. The pattern of a magnetic field can be shown with iron filings or plotting compasses, and the field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.

When current flows through a wire a magnetic field is produced around it, and the field is stronger if the current is larger or the wire is wound into a coil. Winding the wire around a soft iron core produces an electromagnet, which is magnetised while the current flows and demagnetised when it stops — the basis of relays, electric bells and lifting magnets. Reversing the current reverses the poles, and the direction is given by the right-hand grip rule.

Electromagnetic induction works the other way round: moving a magnet into or out of a coil, or moving a coil in a magnetic field, generates a voltage across the coil. A faster movement or a stronger field gives a bigger voltage. This is how generators and dynamos produce electricity. A transformer uses two coils wound on the same iron core to change an alternating voltage: the ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns, and a step-up transformer has more turns on the output coil.

Magnetic flux density is the quantity that describes how strong a magnetic field is: it is the magnetic flux passing through unit area at right angles to the field, B = flux / area, and its direction is the direction of the field line at that point. Magnetic flux is measured in webers (Wb), and the SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 Wb/m2. The Earth's magnetic field at the surface is only about 0.05 mT, while the field of a strong electromagnet or an MRI scanner reaches 1 T or more. Read the unit in the question before you answer: the tesla measures magnetic flux density B, the weber measures magnetic flux, and the henry measures inductance.

Electromagnetic induction: generating a voltage by moving a magnet and a coil relative to each other.
Transformer: two coils on one iron core that change an alternating voltage; the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.

lessons.title: Electrical Power and Safety
lessons.content:
Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred: power = voltage x current, P = VI, measured in watts. Combining this with resistance gives P = I squared R. The energy transferred by an appliance is found from energy = power x time, and domestic electrical energy is sold in kilowatt-hours (kWh), where 1 kWh is the energy a 1 kW appliance transfers in 1 hour.

Domestic circuits are wired in parallel so each appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently. The three-pin plug has a live wire (brown), a neutral wire (blue) and an earth wire (green and yellow). Appliances with metal cases are earthed so that if the live wire touches the case the current flows safely to earth instead of through the user.

A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, and a circuit breaker does the same job with a switch that can be reset. Choosing the correct fuse rating matters: too small and it blows in normal use, too large and it fails to protect. The live wire is connected through the fuse or breaker so that the appliance is isolated from the live supply when it operates.

The heating effect of current is the transfer of electrical energy into thermal energy when a current flows through a resistance, and P = I squared R gives the rate at which that energy appears as heat. Appliances that are meant to get hot use this effect in their heating element: an electric kettle, an iron, a toaster and a room heater all pass a current through a resistance to produce heat, and in a filament lamp the wire is heated until it glows. In other appliances the same heating effect is wasted: the warmth of a motor, a battery charger or a transformer is energy that has not done the useful job, and a fuse is simply a thin wire chosen so that the heating effect melts it when the current becomes dangerously large.

lessons.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.content:
Radioactivity is the spontaneous and random emission of radiation from the unstable nucleus of an atom. There are three primary types of radiation: Alpha (α) particles, which are helium nuclei; Beta (β) particles, which are high-speed electrons; and Gamma (γ) rays, which are high-energy electromagnetic waves. Each type has different penetrating power and ionising ability.

Because radioactive decay is random, we cannot predict when a specific nucleus will decay. However, for a large group of atoms, the rate of decay is predictable. The half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. For example, if a substance has a half-life of 10 years, a 100g sample will be reduced to 50g after 10 years, and then to 25g after another 10 years. A decay graph plots the count rate, the activity or the mass remaining against time, and its curve never reaches zero: the half-life is the time for the value to halve, and it is the same at every halving.

CSEC questions often involve identifying types of radiation from their properties, completing nuclear equations, and using decay curves to determine half-life. Understanding radioactivity is essential for medicine (cancer treatment), archaeology (carbon dating), and energy production (nuclear power).

concepts: Random Nature of Radioactive Decay: the decay of a nucleus is random, so we cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, only the rate for a large group.
Half-life is the time taken for half the nuclei to decay, and it is the same at every halving.
Half-Life and Decay Graphs: a decay graph plots the count rate, the activity or the mass remaining against time, and the half-life is read off as the time for the value to halve.

lessons.title: Work in Establishing the Modern Atom
lessons.content:
For more than two thousand years people have asked what matter is made of, and the answer changed whenever an experiment contradicted the model of the day. The Greek philosopher Democritus proposed tiny indivisible particles he called atoms, but the idea remained a philosophy, because no measurement could test it.

John Dalton's atomic theory, published in 1808, put atoms on a scientific footing: each element is made of identical, indestructible atoms, compounds are combinations of atoms in fixed whole-number ratios, and a chemical reaction only rearranges the atoms. Dalton's model explained the laws of chemical combination, but it treated every atom as a solid sphere with no internal structure.

At the end of the nineteenth century J. J. Thomson's experiments with cathode rays found a much lighter, negatively charged particle inside the atom, the electron. Because an atom as a whole is neutral, Thomson proposed the plum-pudding model: electrons embedded in a ball of positive charge, like fruit in a pudding.

Ernest Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment in 1911 overturned that model. A small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles and some came straight back, which is possible only if the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense centre: the nucleus. Niels Bohr's model extended the picture in 1913 by placing electrons in fixed shells, which explained the sharp spectral lines that the plum-pudding model could not explain.

The pattern of the whole story is that a model survives only while it explains the evidence. Each new experiment kept the parts that still worked and replaced the one part that did not.

Explain the evidence that replaced each model

Thomson's plum-pudding model: electrons embedded in a ball of positive charge.
Rutherford's nucleus: the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense centre, as alpha-particle scattering showed.

lessons.title: Geiger-Marsden Experiment and Nuclear Structure
lessons.content:
In 1909 Ernest Rutherford, working with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil in a vacuum and counted where they went with a zinc sulphide screen that flashed when a particle struck it. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, and the flashes confirmed that they had crossed it with almost no change of direction.

A small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles, and a few alpha particles came straight back towards the source, about one in every 8000. A deflected alpha particle behaves in that way only if it has met a concentrated positive charge: an alpha particle is positive, so a positive nucleus repels it.

From these observations Rutherford concluded that most of the atom is empty space, that all the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus, and that the electrons occupy the rest of the atom. The nucleus is about 10 to the power minus 15 metres across, roughly a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself, which is about 10 to the power minus 10 metres.

The experiment also gave the charge on the nucleus a meaning. The number of units of positive charge equals the atomic number, which is the position of the element in the periodic table, and the electrons that balance that charge must therefore equal it in number.

lessons.title: Atomic Composition and Neutrality
lessons.content:
Every atom is built from three subatomic particles. A proton carries a positive charge and sits in the nucleus. A neutron has no charge and about the same mass as a proton, and it also sits in the nucleus. An electron carries a negative charge, has almost no mass compared with a proton, and occupies the shells around the nucleus.

The number of protons decides which element an atom is: this is the atomic number, Z. The mass number, A, is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, so counted with the protons, the neutrons give the mass number. A nucleus of carbon-12 therefore holds six protons and six neutrons.

An atom as a whole is neutral, because the number of protons equals the number of electrons. Charge is not created or destroyed when an ion forms: an atom gains or loses electrons and the proton count does not change. Losing an electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the particle becomes a positive ion, and gaining an electron gives a negative ion.

Inside the nucleus the protons and neutrons are held together by the strong nuclear force, which acts over the tiny distances between them and is far stronger than the electric repulsion of the protons. The electrons are held to the atom by the electric attraction between their negative charge and the positive nucleus.

lessons.title: Nuclide Notation and Isotopes
lessons.content:
A nuclide is a particular nucleus, and it is written with the mass number as a superscript before the symbol and the atomic number as a subscript. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and it is written with 12 above and 6 below the symbol C, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes of an element behave identically in chemical reactions, because the chemistry is decided by the electrons and isotopes have the same number of electrons. They differ in mass number, in density, and in the rate at which they take part in physical processes such as diffusion.

Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium with one proton and no neutrons, deuterium with one proton and one neutron, and tritium with one proton and two neutrons. The relative atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes, which is why the relative atomic mass of chlorine is about 35.5 although no single chlorine atom has that mass.

Some isotopes are radioactive and others are stable. Carbon-14 is radioactive and is used for dating, while carbon-12 is stable and makes up almost all the carbon on Earth. How many electrons an ion has is found from the atomic number, not from the mass number.

lessons.title: Shell Model and the Periodic Table
lessons.content:
In the shell model the electrons of an atom are arranged in shells around the nucleus. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second and third hold up to 8, and the shells fill from the inside outwards. Sodium has eleven electrons and the configuration 2, 8, 1.

An element's place in the periodic table follows from its shells. The group number equals the number of electrons in the outer shell, so every element of group 1 has one outer electron and every element of group 7 has seven. The period number equals the number of occupied shells, so the elements of period 3 have electrons in three shells.

The outer electrons decide how an element behaves chemically. Sodium with one outer electron loses it to form a positive ion, and chlorine with seven outer electrons gains one to form a negative ion, so both end up with a full outer shell. Electrons in a full outer shell are held firmly and are not easily removed.

The noble gases of group 8 have a full outer shell, so they are unreactive: helium has 2 outer electrons and the rest of the group have 8. The shell model therefore explains the shape of the periodic table rather than merely describing it. It also shows its own limit, because it says nothing about the nucleus and cannot explain radioactivity.

lessons.title: Marie Curie's Work and Radioactivity
lessons.content:
In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged a photographic plate even when they had not been exposed to sunlight. Marie Curie took up the puzzle, and with her husband Pierre Curie showed that the rays came from the uranium atoms themselves rather than from a chemical reaction, and she gave the process the name radioactivity.

The Curies processed tonnes of pitchblende, a uranium ore, and in 1898 they separated two new elements that were far more radioactive than uranium: polonium and radium. Radium was about a million times more radioactive than uranium, and isolating it took years of chemical work, with tonnes of ore yielding a fraction of a gram.

Becquerel and the Curies shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, and Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911 for the discovery of radium and polonium and for her study of the nature of these new elements. She was the first person to win a Nobel Prize twice.

The discovery changed both physics and medicine. Radium was used in early cancer treatment, and radioactive isotopes later became medical tracers. The work also showed the hazards: the Curies and their assistants handled radioactive material without shielding and their health suffered, which is why the safety precautions used today exist.

lessons.title: Effects of Electric and Magnetic Fields on Emissions
lessons.content:
An electric field exerts a force on any charged particle and none on a neutral one, so the three emissions behave differently between two charged plates. A beam of alpha particles bends towards the negative plate, because an alpha particle is positive. A beam of beta particles bends towards the positive plate, and so in the opposite direction to the alpha beam.

The amount of bending depends on the charge and the mass of the particle. A beta particle is deflected far more than an alpha particle: it is negative and it is much lighter, and a light particle is deflected more by the same force. Gamma rays pass through undeflected, because they carry no charge.

A magnetic field bends charged particles too, and the force acts at right angles to both the field and the direction of travel. Alpha particles bend one way and beta particles bend the opposite way, because their charges are opposite, and the beta deflection is again much the greater. Gamma rays are not deflected by a magnetic field at all.

Deflections like these are how the three emissions were told apart in the laboratory, and the same principle is used today to focus a beam of charged particles or to separate ions of different mass.

lessons.title: Interpreting Nuclear Reactions
lessons.content:
A nuclear reaction is written as an equation with the mass number and the atomic number of each nuclide, and the equation must balance on both counts. In the alpha decay of uranium-238 the equation is uranium-238 giving thorium-234 plus an alpha particle: the mass numbers balance because 238 equals 234 plus 4, and the atomic numbers balance because 92 equals 90 plus 2.

In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by one. Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 plus a beta particle: 14 balances with 14 plus 0, and 6 balances with 7 plus minus 1. The beta particle is written with a mass number of 0 and an atomic number of minus 1, because it is an electron.

Gamma emission is written with no change to either number, which is why a gamma ray is often left out of a decay equation. In every case the particle missing from a partly written equation is found by making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers add up on each side.

The same rule covers artificial transmutation. In 1919 Rutherford passed alpha particles through nitrogen gas and found that nitrogen-14 had changed into oxygen-17 plus a proton, and an equation of that kind identifies the product of any bombardment.

lessons.title: Applications of Radio-Isotopes
lessons.content:
A radio-isotope is chosen for a job by its half-life and by the radiation it emits. For use inside the body the half-life should be short, so that the dose does not last, and the emission should be gamma rays, which leave the body instead of being absorbed by it. Technetium-99m is used as a tracer in medical imaging, where a gamma camera follows it through an organ, and this is the commonest use in medicine.

Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays and is used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells, and it is also used to sterilise medical equipment and food. A strongly ionising alpha emitter is used where its short range is an advantage: americium-241 is the alpha source in a smoke detector, where its alpha particles ionise the air and allow a small current to flow.

In industry a beta or gamma source measures the thickness of paper, plastic or metal as the material passes between the source and a detector, and a tracer added to a pipeline shows up a leak. In agriculture phosphorus-32 follows the uptake of fertiliser by a plant, and radiation is used to breed new varieties of crop.

In archaeology carbon-14 is used for dating once-living material, because a living thing takes in carbon until it dies and its carbon-14 then decays with a half-life of about 5700 years, so the activity left shows how long ago it died. Uranium-238, with a half-life of about 4500 million years, dates rocks.

lessons.title: Energy from Nuclear Reactions
lessons.content:
A nuclear reaction releases energy because the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants. The difference is called the mass defect, and the small loss of mass appears as energy according to the equation E = mc squared, where c is the speed of light. Because the speed of light is large, a tiny mass corresponds to a very large amount of energy.

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus. A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes unstable and splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing two or three neutrons and a large amount of energy. The neutrons released by fission can cause further fissions, so the process can become a chain reaction: in a reactor the chain reaction is controlled, and in a weapon it is not.

Nuclear fusion is the joining of light nuclei. In the Sun hydrogen nuclei join to form helium, releasing energy and needing extremely high temperatures and pressures to bring the nuclei close enough to fuse. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission and produces less long-lived radioactive waste, but it has not yet been made to work as a power source on Earth.

For the same mass of fuel a nuclear reaction releases far more energy than burning coal, oil or gas, which is why a nuclear power station needs only a small mass of uranium each year.

lessons.title: Utilisation of Nuclear Energy
lessons.content:
A nuclear power station uses the heat from a controlled fission chain reaction to make steam, which drives turbines that turn generators. The fuel is uranium, usually enriched in uranium-235 and sealed inside fuel rods. A moderator such as graphite or water slows the fast neutrons down so that they can cause further fission, control rods of boron or cadmium absorb neutrons, and a coolant carries the heat away to the boiler.

Each part of the reactor has one job, and the design is meant to keep the reaction from running away. The control rods are pushed in to absorb more neutrons and reduce the power and pulled out to raise it; thick concrete and steel shielding stops neutrons and gamma rays reaching the people outside; and the used fuel is stored under water, which removes its heat and shields the radiation.

The advantages of nuclear power are large: a small mass of fuel gives a very large amount of energy, and generating electricity this way does not produce carbon dioxide or the other gases that cause acid rain. The disadvantages are large too. The used fuel is radioactive waste that stays hazardous for thousands of years, so it must be stored and shielded; a reactor is expensive to build and to decommission; uranium is a non-renewable fuel; and an accident releases radioactive material into the surroundings.

The decision is a judgement about which risks a country will accept. Jamaica generates its electricity mainly from oil and gas and has no nuclear power station, so nuclear power is an option for countries with the grid, the money and the regulatory system to run it safely. Radiation safety itself rests on three ideas: shielding, distance and time.
